lead: The Friis transmission equation gives the power a receiving antenna collects from a transmitter at distance d in free space. It multiplies the transmit power by both antenna gains and divides by the spreading of the wave. Written in decibels it becomes a plain sum of gains and losses, the link budget, which is checked against the receiver’s sensitivity to find the margin. Wi-Fi, point-to-point microwave and satellite links are all planned this way; radar uses the same idea twice, out to the target and back.
prereq: You need: gain (antenna parameters), effective aperture (receiving antenna) and the far-field distance (near and far field).

items: An isotropic source of power P<sub>t</sub> spreads it over a sphere of area 4πd², giving S = P<sub>t</sub>/(4πd²) at distance d.
A transmitting antenna of gain G<sub>t</sub> pointed at the receiver raises that density by G<sub>t</sub>: S = P<sub>t</sub> G<sub>t</sub>/(4πd²). The product P<sub>t</sub>G<sub>t</sub> is the EIRP.
The receiving antenna collects S times its effective area A<sub>er</sub> = G<sub>r</sub> λ²/4π: P<sub>r</sub> = S A<sub>er</sub>.

blocks.text: Pr = Pt Gt Gr (λ / 4πd)². Pr, Pt in W; Gt, Gr as ratios, not dB; λ and d in the same unit

Writing both gains as apertures gives the aperture form Pr = Pt Aet Aer / (λ² d²). The two forms tell different stories. For fixed gains, received power falls as λ² gets smaller, that is with frequency squared; for fixed apertures (dishes of fixed size) it rises with frequency squared, because each dish’s gain grows faster than the spreading loss.
The factor (4πd/λ)² is the free-space path loss (FSPL). It is not absorption by the air: it is the share of the spreading wave that an isotropic receiving antenna happens to catch.
FSPL(dB) = 32.44 + 20 log₁₀ fMHz + 20 log₁₀ dkm. f in MHz and d in km; the constant is 20 log₁₀(4π × 10⁹/c)
Convert powers to dBm, P(dBm) = 10 log₁₀(P/1 mW), and gains to dBi. The product becomes a sum:
Pr = Pt + Gt + Gr − FSPL − Lt − Lr − Lmisc. all in dBm or dB; Lt and Lr are the feeder (cable and connector) losses at each end; Lmisc covers polarization, pointing and radome losses
In dB form, EIRP(dBm) = P<sub>t</sub> + G<sub>t</sub> − L<sub>t</sub>. Regulators limit EIRP in each band, so fitting a higher-gain antenna can force a lower transmit power.

The receiver’s sensitivity Psens is the weakest signal it can use at its specified error rate. The link margin M = Pr − Psens must be positive; designers keep a fade margin of 10 to 30 dB or more for rain, multipath and misalignment, depending on how reliable the link must be. Solving the budget for the largest FSPL that still leaves the required margin gives the maximum range.

items: Far field at both ends: d > 2D²/λ for the larger antenna, and d ≫ λ.
Free space: a clear line of sight, no ground reflection, no multipath, no rain or gas absorption. Real paths add these (see ground, sky and space wave propagation).
Matched antennas: both pointed at each other, co-polarized and impedance matched; otherwise multiply by the PLF and by 1 − |Γ|² at each end.
Consistent units: d and λ in the same unit; gains as ratios in the product form and in dB only in the dB form.

blocks.text: FSPL grows by 20 log₁₀ 2 = 6.02 dB for every doubling of distance, and by the same 6.02 dB for every doubling of frequency with fixed gains.

figure.caption: The worked example’s 6 GHz hop as a level diagram: 1 W (30 dBm) loses 2 dB in the feeder, the 34.95 dBi dish lifts it to 62.95 dBm EIRP, 40 km of free space takes 140.04 dB, and the far dish and feeder leave −44.1 dBm, 30.9 dB above the −75 dBm sensitivity.

A dashed line at minus 75 dBm marks the sensitivity and an arrow marks the 30.9 dB margin.

examples.question: A 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi link has P<sub>t</sub> = 100 mW, 0 dBi antennas at both ends, d = 100 m, 2 dB of cable and connector loss in all, and a receiver sensitivity of −90 dBm. Find λ, FSPL, the received power and the link margin.
steps: FSPL = 20 log₁₀(4πd/λ) = 20 log₁₀(4π × 100/0.125) = 20 log₁₀(10 053) = 80.05 dB. Check with the MHz–km form: 32.44 + 67.60 + (−20.00) = 80.04 dB.
examples.answer: λ = 0.125 m; FSPL = 80.05 dB; P<sub>r</sub> = −62.0 dBm; margin 28.0 dB, so the link works with room for walls and fading.

examples.question: A 6 GHz point-to-point microwave hop is 40 km long. Each end has a 1.2 m dish with aperture efficiency 0.55 and 2 dB of feeder loss; the transmitter gives 1 W and the receiver needs −75 dBm. Find the dish gain, the FSPL, the received power and the margin, and check that Friis applies.
steps: Dish gain: G = e<sub>ap</sub>(πD/λ)² = 0.55 × (π × 1.2/0.05)² = 0.55 × 5685 = 3127, that is 34.95 dBi.
M = −44.14 − (−75) = 30.86 dB, about 31 dB of fade margin.
Far field: 2D²/λ = 2 × 1.44/0.05 = 57.6 m, far less than 40 km, so the far-field formula is valid.
examples.answer: G = 34.95 dBi per dish; FSPL = 140.0 dB; P<sub>r</sub> = −44.1 dBm; margin 30.9 dB.

traps: Dropping one of the two gains. Friis has both G<sub>t</sub> and G<sub>r</sub>.
Putting dB values into the ratio form, or ratios into the dB form. A 20 dBi antenna enters the product form as 100 and the dB form as 20.
Using d in km with λ in m in 20 log₁₀(4πd/λ). Only the 32.44 form takes MHz and km.
Treating FSPL as the only loss. Feeder, mismatch, polarization and pointing losses are added on top.
Getting the margin backwards. M = P<sub>r</sub> − P<sub>sens</sub>; with P<sub>sens</sub> = −90 dBm and P<sub>r</sub> = −62 dBm the margin is +28 dB.

quiz.q: State the Friis transmission equation and define each symbol with its unit.
quiz.a: P<sub>r</sub> = P<sub>t</sub>G<sub>t</sub>G<sub>r</sub>(λ/4πd)²: powers in W, gains as ratios, λ and d in metres (any common unit).

quiz.q: Define EIRP and give its dB form.
quiz.a: The power an isotropic antenna would need to give the same peak power density: EIRP = P<sub>t</sub>G<sub>t</sub>; in dB, P<sub>t</sub>(dBm) + G<sub>t</sub>(dBi) − L<sub>t</sub>(dB).

quiz.q: Why does doubling the frequency add about 6 dB to the FSPL?
quiz.a: FSPL = (4πd/λ)² and λ = c/f, so FSPL ∝ f². Doubling f multiplies it by 4, which is 10 log₁₀ 4 = 6.02 dB.

quiz.q: Why must a practical link keep a positive margin rather than exactly zero?
quiz.a: At zero margin the signal is exactly at sensitivity, so any fade, rain, extra cable loss or misalignment breaks the link. The margin is the reserve for those.

quiz.q: A 5 GHz link has P<sub>t</sub> = 20 dBm, 6 dBi antennas at both ends, d = 50 m and 1 dB of other loss. Find FSPL and P<sub>r</sub> (λ = 0.06 m).
If the distance of a link doubles, how does the received power change?
quiz.a: FSPL ∝ d², so it rises by 6.02 dB and the received power falls by 6.02 dB (to one quarter).

quiz.q: Two dishes of fixed size are moved from a 6 GHz link to an 18 GHz link of the same length. Does the received power rise or fall, and by how much?
quiz.a: From the aperture form P<sub>r</sub> = P<sub>t</sub>A<sub>et</sub>A<sub>er</sub>/(λ²d²), it rises as 1/λ². Tripling f raises it by 20 log₁₀ 3 = 9.54 dB in free space (each dish gains 9.54 dB, the FSPL grows by 9.54 dB); rain loss, much larger at 18 GHz, is extra.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real link planning adds measured path-loss models (two-ray ground reflection, Okumura–Hata for cellular, ITU-R models for rain and gases) on top of free space, and satellite links add the noise temperature of the receiving system to work in carrier-to-noise ratio rather than received power. Radar uses Friis twice with the target’s radar cross section in between, which is why its range grows only as the fourth root of power. Search next for “ITU-R P.525”, “rain fade margin” and “radar range equation”.
